title: CBA gives away AI security tool in ‘automated defence’ to stop hackers
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank has designed a custom-built artificial intelligence security tool to comb through billions of lines of code to search for vulnerabilities – allowing businesses to apply fixes before hackers find and exploit them.
The bank is giving the tool away for free to help stop machine-speed hackers from crippling supermarkets, medical clinics and small businesses.
It was developed after CBA invested more than $1bn last financial year to defend customers from scams, fraud and cyber crime.
The Australian Signals Directorate has called for more AI-powered tools to fight cyber attacks after it reported an 80 per cent surge in malicious activity in the past year. Coles is the latest company to confirm it is investigating a “cybersecurity incident”.
The ASD also found that while most vulnerability exploitation occurs within two weeks, some were successfully exploited within 48 hours of a patch or fix, and warns that AI will accelerate attacks further.
“We need AI tools to help automate our defences and stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” ASD director-general Abigail Bradshaw said.
The move by CBA is believed to be an Australian first. While major banks and telcos have historically borne the brunt of high-profile data breaches, threat actors are increasingly targeting smaller businesses and everyday infrastructure, including local grocery stores, doctors clinics and health clinics.
CBA chief executive Matt Comyn said cyber attacks were the “most challenging non-financial risk” for businesses.
“Certainly I’ve never seen an acceleration in any risk to match,” he said. “I’m extremely worried about this risk. I think there would be tens of billions of dollars of investment that will be required across the economy, and that’ll be true in every country.” CBA chief security officer Nicola Nicol said the CodeCheck tool allowed companies to defend themselves and identify bugs 24/7.
“With thousands of engineers working across systems powered by around 2.5 billion lines of code, we’ve seen first-hand how AI can help identify potential vulnerabilities earlier,” she said.
CodeCheck is available as a plug-in for tools such as OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code, acting as a secure development harness that guides models through a structured process to find and surface vulnerabilities before code reaches production. Users have to pay for their associated token usage. “Cyber security is a shared challenge, and strengthening Australia’s cyber resilience requires us all to play a part. As cyber criminals increasingly use AI, we also need to put AI to work on the defensive side,” Ms Nicol said.
